title.narrative: Lao PDR Green Resilient Growth DPO 2

description.narrative: Most recently, Lao PDR experienced widespread floods between July and September 2018, which significantly impacted its people and economy. To build long-term prosperity, Lao's growth pattern needs to continue shifting to a better-managed, more diversified and sustainable green growth model. The World Bank is supporting Lao PDR's green growth transformation through analytic and advisory services and a series of three programmatic green growth development policy operations (GGDPO). The program development objective of GGDPO2 is to achieve fiscal sustainability and financial sector stability, adopt green growth planning and monitoring, and introduce green growth tools and principles in priority sectors. The program's three pillars complement one another to improve the growth prospects of the country and help make economic activities cleaner, more resource-efficient, and more resilient. Pillar 1 supports economic management actions to address key macroeconomic risks. Pillar 2 establishes policy-level instruments for green growth planning, financing, and monitoring. Pillar 3 aims to incorporate green growth principles in selected sectors, including measures for sustainably using the country's key natural assets (water, forests, and biodiversity), building resilience of infrastructure to climate risks, and promoting cleaner, more efficient production and consumption by regulating pollution.
To support the Government of Lao PDR in achieving fiscal sustainability and consolidating its path towards green growth.

title.narrative: Indicator 1. Tax buoyancy (i.e., tax revenue as a share of GDP) increases

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Not achieved.</strong> Not only was the target not achieved, outcomes went in the opposite direction to what was expected.  Instead of rising, the tax to GDP ratio declined from 12.4 percent in 2016 to 9.6 percent (projected) in 2022.</p>

title.narrative: Indicator 5: Public debt (as a percentage of GDP) decreases

comment.narrative:
<p><strong>Not achieved.</strong> We note that public debt data has been revised at various points in the last few years and the public debt ratio to GDP varies depending on whether guarantees are included or not. However, the trend has been upward for both versions. Rather than decreasing, the public debt (excluding guarantees) ratio has increased, from 46.8 percent of GDP in 2016 to as much as 79 percent in 2022 (projected).  This suggests that the link between the relevant PAs and the RI was not strong.  Other factors with a bearing on the public debt ratio offset any impact that the PAs might have had.   </p>

<p>despite te approval of the Public Debt Law in 2018 (DPO2, PA3), there has been slow progress in the development of implementing instructions, a Public Debt Management Strategy, and a medium-term borrowing plan (envisaged as DPO3, indicative trigger 3).</p>

<p>The GOL has taken several actions to reduce the high debt burden even though the DPO was discontinued. For example, spending is being controlle through a cut-back in foreign financed public investments. The authorities have also been in discussion on debt restructuring with key bilateral creditors. As part of the Sustainable Development Finance Policy (SDFP) engagement with the World Bank, the GOL has st a cap on non-concessional borrowing for the last two years and has complied with the relevant ceilings.</p>

<p> </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 2. Public sector wage bill (as a percentage of GDP) decreases

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved.</strong> The authorities have maintained the same wage multiplier since 2017. As a result, the public wage bill to GDP declined from 7.0 percent of GDP in 2017 to 6.0 percent in 2021.</p>

title.narrative: Indicator 8: Increase in number of revenue sources of the EPF

baseline.value: 3 - contributions from development partners, contributions from business, endowment fund

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Fully achieved.</strong> ???????At present, revenue from the following five sources is available to the EPF: (i) State Budget, (ii) Contributions under the concession agreement of hydropower and mining investment projects, (iii) Direct grants from national and international organizations, (iv) Interest and profits generated from capital investments; and (v) Fines and indemnities related to environment damaging activities, such as wastewater discharges. </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 6: Public reporting of compliance with regulations of the Capital Adequacy Ratio, by type of banks

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Not achieved</strong>. The BOL started to publish the Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) for the banking sector, as one of 7 core financial soundness indicators (FSIs), in 2017.  Further disaggregation of the CAR, by type of bank, as envisagedin the results matrix, will not be available by 2022.  Government decided not to move forward with disaggregating FSIs until the restructuring of two distressed state-owned banks is completed.    </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 11: Share of investment projects in the mining, energy, and transport sectors that require an ESIA with complete disclosure of relevant information through the integrated database and public

comment.narrative:
<p><strong>Exceeded.</strong> The target is achieved with 100% of investment projects in the mining, energy and transport sectors that required an ESIA disclosing relevant information through the public information platform prior to approval. ESIA reports from the category 2 investment projects (total of 88) subject to MONRE review are uploaded on the <em>website</em> for public consultation and participation (as required by the ESIA decree).  The target was set at 70% so it is exceeded since all relevant projects have complied.</p>
<p> </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 4: Percentage of central government agencies issuing tenders according to the new Public Procurement Law by 2022

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Not achieved.</strong> It has proved difficult to measure adherence to all aspects of the Law in all tenders due to limited human and IT system capacity. Monitoring of tenders using the new tools will be done through the Public Procurement website completed in June 2022. This implies that monitoring will take place in the second half of the year.   </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 13: Number of river basins that establish the minimum flow requirements set out in their respective River Basin Plan

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Partially achieved. </strong>Eight river basin management plans (RBMP) have been developed, and are likely to be approved by the end of this year by the Minister which include the value of minimum flow requirements. </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 12: Share of approved road maintenance projects with climate resilience and disaster risk considerations envisaged in the Annual Road Maintenance Plan & Budget verified by technical audits

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Fully achieved.</strong> 100% of road maintenance projects incorporate climate resilience and disaster risk measures. About 50% of technical audits on maintenance projects have been done so far. </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 16: Number of inspections by MAF of pesticide sellers for compliance with pesticide regulations per year

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Fully achieved.</strong> The ICR mission was informed by the MAF in November 2021 that there were 85 inspectors throughout the country, and each inspector has conducted at least 2-3 inspections. Based on this, it would appear that the inspections target of 140 has been met.   </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 10: Number of SEAs undertaken for public policies, programs, and strategic plans

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Exceeded.</strong> Two SEAs have been undertaken for the Hydropower Sector Strategy, and the National Green Growth Strategy.</p>

title.narrative: Indicator 15: Number of national parks established where progress in reaching management objectives is at least moderately satisfactory, as measured by the Management Effectiveness Tracking Tool

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Fully achieved</strong>. Nakai Nam Theun and Nam Et-Phou Louey were established as national parks and their management objectives in 2021 was rated satisfactory, as per the assessment by the Management Effectiveness Tracking Tool (METT). </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 17: Number of Priority Pollution Watch Sites for which monitoring reports (including at least PM2.5, arsenic, lead, and pathogens concentrations) are updated and publicly disclosed annually

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved.</strong> Monitoring reports for four provinces (Vientiane, Bolikhamxay, Savannakhet and Champasack) covering PPWSs with parameters including PM2.5, arsenic, lead, and pathogens concentrations were updated and submitted to PCD for disclosure through MONRE dedicated website. These four provinces were also part of the 10 provinces that published Provincial Pollution Reports for public disclosure. The PPWSs were selected based on the number of factories, tourism sites, mining concessions, wastewater discharge among others. The monitoring reports will be uploaded on the MONRE dedicated website by mid 2022, following the completion of the website. It remains to be seen whether these reports will be updated and disclosed annually.</p>

title.narrative: Indicator 18: Percentage of legally imported paint brands offering unleaded paint in the national market

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Achieved. </strong>As per the 2019 PCD report, 150 samples were analyzed to assess the lead element in paints.Of these, 95 samples of imported paint, only two samples or 2% are beyond the standards (90ppm). This was a good achievement following GOL’s policies under GGDPO1&2, which is further strengthened by MONRE’s decision 4566 providing technical guidance on lead content in paint and coating materials. This 2% could also be attributed to old stocks or illegal imports (as the data are based on market sampling). </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 14: Increase in number of hectares within PFAs with certified Sustainable Forest Management operations based on Lao PDR regulations

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Partially achieved.</strong> As of December 2021, 99,607 hectares of forest area have already been certified. Planned forest certification shows that 152,043 ha of certified forest area are under implementation, thus taking the total certified area to 251,650 hectares, which will be above the target of 230,000 ha, by the end of 2022. Government appears to be on trackto achieve the target for this indicator but we cannot be certain of full achievement since the ICR is being done prior to the scheduled end of the project period of December 2022. </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 7: Disclosure of M&E results of the green growth priorities established in the National Green Growth Strategy, as part of the public consultation process of the 9th NSEDP (20212025)

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Fully achieved. </strong>M&E indicators with green growth priorities have been included in the 9th NSEDP, the NGGS, and the GG planning manual and disclosed as part of the 9th NSEDP's consultation process. </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 9: Disclosure of annual financial audit of the EPF

comment.narrative:
<p><strong>Fully achieved.</strong> The EPF website has published:</p>

<ul>
 <li>two financial audits conducted by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) for the years 2019 and year 2020</li>
 <li>the 2018 financial report, under the LENS2/WB project</li>
</ul>

<p> </p>

title.narrative: Indicator 3: Capable of recording and reporting of GoLs financial transactions consistent with the IMF-GFSM2014 by 2022

comment.narrative: <p><strong>Partially achieved. </strong>Progress is being made by MOF to achieved the target. The Chart of Accounts is being revised to be consistent with IMF GFSM2014 and is expected to be finalized in 2022, after which parts of it will be piloted in the existing government financial information system. The fully revised COA is expected to be implemented with the GOL new Integrated Financial Management Information System in 2024.</p>
